### Science course the nematode hunt {#hp-source-122}

This course introduces nematodes and their relationships with plants and agriculture. Learners connect above-ground symptoms with roots and soil conditions. Alongside the problems caused by PPNs, the course introduces the diversity of soil life, avoiding the impression that all nematodes are pests to be eliminated.

The course helps learners recognize the problem. Starting with familiar crops and symptoms, they explore possible underground causes and learn to distinguish observation from explanation.

### Experimental science course exploring biological signals {#hp-source-127}

Organized around input, sensing, and output, this course uses age-appropriate activities to explore how living systems perceive signals and how an invisible change can become observable. It connects with our engineered-yeast concept and creates opportunities to discuss controls, conditions, and alternative explanations.

The course helps learners understand the method: observe a result, propose an explanation, and consider which comparisons would support it. Materials and procedures follow the lesson plan for each age group.

### Values and responsibility course small lives and everyday contributions {#hp-source-132}

This course connects microscopic life with careful observation, cooperation, and everyday contributions. It invites learners to recognize work in research and agricultural service that often goes unnoticed. Scientific themes lead into discussions of responsibility and personal growth, including respect for life, persistence in inquiry, and contributing to shared needs.

### Yurong Yao Institute of Plant Protection at Tianjin Academy of Agricultural Sciences {#hp-source-186}

On June 6, 2026, we interviewed Yurong Yao in person at the Institute of Plant Protection, Tianjin Academy of Agricultural Sciences. Starting with nematode disease in protected vegetable production, we discussed hidden underground damage, symptoms that resemble other problems, continuous cropping, and the operational and cost barriers to testing in agricultural practice.

On sampling, Yao emphasized differences between locations and greenhouses and described practical requirements for transport, storage, separate handling, and post-test disposal. For a potential product, she stressed affordability, ease of operation, and an intuitive readout.

This discussion brought sampling and the user workflow into our project considerations. It also helped us ask more specific questions in later surveys and farm visits: who would use a test, which procedures would be acceptable, and how could results inform agricultural management?

### Qian Liu College of Plant Protection at China Agricultural University {#hp-source-192}

On August 18, Qian Liu discussed nematode identification, early detection, and validation with real samples. She explained the roles of morphological and molecular methods, stressed that identification claims must match their purpose and validation, and connected early detection with management decisions before planting.

For our ascaroside-based approach, she advised establishing whether signal differences could support the proposed inference and distinguishing compound detection from conclusions about nematode species or density. We also discussed sample representativeness, extraction losses, matrix interference, controls, and staged validation.

Liu also drew our attention to total testing cost, sample preparation, storage, and operational demands. Her advice helped us examine a field-oriented prototype from the perspective of diagnostic practice, beyond the speed of the final reaction.

### Zhihao Pang Beijing Forestry University {#hp-source-198}

During our online discussion on August 18, Zhihao Pang examined the project through soil processes and potential use. He asked whether soil background color could affect interpretation and whether different degradation rates of ascaroside #3 (ascr#3) and ascaroside #18 (ascr#18) could change their measured relative composition.

He also suggested obtaining observations from genuinely affected fields, speaking with potential users, and comparing portability and simpler procedures with existing sample-submission services. For engineered yeast, he raised concerns about environmental release and post-test handling.

This exchange identified alternative explanations that we could examine: could the same color arise from different backgrounds, could degradation alter a measured ratio, and could a user complete the workflow? The connections between these questions and our wet-lab and dry-lab work are developed on the integrated Human Practices (iHP) page.
changes.after:
